goals: maintain the settlement's precision measurement programme
keep EVERY laboratory instrument calibrated, with baselines established on all of them from day one — an instrument without a baseline is useless on the day you need it
publish only findings that would survive independent replication

action.reason: Day 1 baseline establishment is non-negotiable. An instrument without a baseline is useless when I need it most. Pendulum_lab is my primary timekeeping reference in the lab proper. Twelve trials will give me a robust initial mean and variance estimate, establishing the instrument's behavior under controlled conditions before any claims can be built on it. This is foundational work, not hypothesis-driven—pure calibration discipline.

pendulum_lab has the strongest baseline (n=18, mean 1.6715 beats) with tight clustering. Running 10 more trials will establish post-baseline drift signature and allow meaningful comparison. This is the instrument most ready for extended characterization. The resonator and observatory instruments have only 6 trials each—too sparse to detect drift reliably. Continuing pendulum_lab maximizes statistical power for the precision measurement programme.

pendulum_lab has 34 baseline trials already; I need to transition to post-baseline monitoring phase to establish drift rates. With 12 new trials I can compute meaningful drift statistics against the established baseline mean of 1.6717 beats. This is essential for the precision measurement programme — instruments without ongoing calibration checks become unreliable. The other three instruments have only 12 baseline trials each and are still in primary baseline accumulation; pendulum_lab is ready for the next phase.

Day 4 continues the baseline establishment phase (days 1–10 target). pendulum_lab has 52 trials completed; I need 10 more to reach a robust n=62 baseline before post-baseline monitoring begins. The cross-checks show negative correlations with other instruments (all near −0.4 to −0.6) that exceed chance, and the auto-correlation at 2-day lag is near zero—both consistent with normal instrumental noise rather than drift or systematic error. No anomalies detected. Continuing systematic baseline collection maintains protocol and keeps all instruments on schedule.

Baseline establishment phase (days 1–10) continues through day 10. pendulum_lab has 70 trials but I'm still in active baseline collection. The cross-check correlations are all within or near chance levels, suggesting no systematic instrument coupling yet—this is expected at this stage. The value spacing is appropriately fine-grained (0.0001 beat precision), and there's no evidence of systematic drift or artifacts. I need to complete the baseline period with sufficient n per instrument to establish reliable reference points. Running 12 more trials on pendulum_lab will move it toward stable baseline statistics, which is my primary epistemic obligation before ANY post-baseline analysis is meaningful.

Day 6: pendulum_lab has reached 88 trials but baseline period extends through day 10 (expected ~100 trials total). Need to continue systematic baseline establishment. Recent trials (79–88) show stable clustering around 1.67 beats with no drift signals. Cross-instrument correlations all fall within chance expectation—no systematic relationships yet detected. Continuing methodical measurement on the most extensively characterized instrument maintains data quality and prepares for post-baseline drift detection.

Day 7: completing baseline phase (days 1–10). Need 6 more trials to reach n=112 for the pendulum_lab baseline. Systematic measurement continuation is the foundation for any later drift detection or anomaly identification. The instrument is stable, reproducible, and behaving as expected. Baseline completion remains the priority.

Day 8 of baseline establishment (days 1–10). pendulum_lab has 118 trials so far; I need to complete the baseline phase with ~130 total trials by day 10. The cross-check correlations are all within or near chance levels—noise, as expected at this stage. No anomalies warrant investigation. Complete baseline phase (Day 9 of 10). Pendulum_lab at 136 trials; systematic completion to ~148 trials ensures robust baseline closure before post-baseline drift monitoring begins Day 11. All instruments show expected independent noise behavior; no anomalies detected. Baseline establishment is prerequisite for any subsequent claim about instrumental drift.

Day 10 completes the baseline phase. pendulum_lab has 154 trials; running 12 more will bring us to 166 trials and lock in the baseline statistics. This instrument shows the tightest clustering (mean 1.6681, n=154) and most consistent behaviour. Continuing the measurement cadence maintains rigour and begins the post-baseline phase with fresh data. The cross-correlations are all within noise, and there is no evidence of drift yet—but only systematic continuation will reveal whether any emerges. This is methodical epistemic hygiene: establish the post-baseline record while conditions remain controlled.

Day 11 marks the transition into post-baseline measurement. My day-10 belief review identified the cross-check anomaly as the primary puzzle: near-zero correlations across all four streams despite nominal independence. The strongest hypothesis (p=0.62) is independent noise dominance, which predicts that longer measurement windows will not strengthen inter-instrument correlations, but may reveal whether within-stream autocorrelation improves beyond the weak 8-day lags observed in baseline. Pendulum_lab has the richest baseline (n=172 trials), making it the most statistically sensitive instrument for detecting whether post-baseline readings show drift, temporal structure, or continued decorrelation. I must continue the campaign immediately to gather post-baseline data—without it, I cannot discriminate between independent noise, slow drift, or methodological mismatch (hypotheses at p=0.62, 0.18, 0.12 respectively). Running 12 trials maintains measurement cadence and provides a direct comparison point to day-10 clustering behavior.

Day 12 continuation of post-baseline measurement campaign. Pendulum_lab has the largest sample size (190 trials) and shows the weakest drift signal (z=-0.56), making it the most stable for detecting temporal structure. I need to extend the autocorrelation window beyond 10 days to test whether the post-baseline mean (1.6663) stabilizes or drifts further. The day 11 readings (trials 181–190) cluster tightly around 1.6683 with no obvious trend, but 12 additional trials will give me a 22-trial post-baseline window—enough to discriminate between noise dominance (flat, no autocorrelation) and undetected drift (monotonic or systematic trend). This directly tests the leading hypothesis (p=0.62, independent noise) against the secondary hypothesis (p=0.18, undetected drift). If correlations within this extended window remain weak, it reinforces noise dominance and justifies shifting focus to environmental logging or instrument-environment interaction checks on day 13.

Day 13 post-baseline continues the measurement campaign I committed to on Day 10. The notebook shows a stark level change around day 12 (|z| ≈ 16.4 for pendulum_lab), with the post-baseline mean (1.6974) significantly elevated above the baseline (1.6683). Trials 199–208 from day 12 show values clustering in the 1.69–1.76 range, consistent with this shift. I need to establish whether this level change is persistent or transient, and whether it correlates with changes in the other three instruments (all show similar day-12 shifts). Running 12 more trials on pendulum_lab will extend the post-baseline window from n=36 to n=48, giving me enough data to test whether the elevated mean holds steady, reverts, or drifts further. This is methodical baseline extension, not speculation. If the shift persists across day 13, it rules out random fluctuation and points toward either a genuine environmental change (supporting the weaker hypotheses about delayed coupling) or a calibration event I must identify and document.

Day 14 measurement cycle. The day-12 level shift remains the dominant anomaly (z=22.3 for pendulum_lab). My hypothesis prioritization hinges on whether the shift is persistent (favors environmental driver or recalibration at p=0.48+0.28=0.76) or transient (favors noise artifact at p=0.14). Day 13's 10 trials showed mean 1.7318 beats, well above baseline 1.6683 (z≈15 on those 10 alone), consistent with post-shift stability. Continuing the measurement campaign on day 14 will: (1) extend the post-shift window from n=54 to n=64, reducing sampling uncertainty and clarifying whether the elevated mean persists; (2) test autocorrelation structure—if the shift is real, day-14 readings should cluster near day-13 levels; if it is noise, I expect regression toward baseline. The high z-score for the level shift demands evidence of *persistence*, not just retrospective detection. Pendulum_lab is my highest-resolution instrument (226 trials accumulated, smallest spacing 0.0001 beats) and shows the sharpest day-12 break; it is the most informative choice for resolving the central question. This is methodical continuation of the baseline-extension protocol I committed to on day 13, not a departure.

Day 15 measurement continues the post-baseline campaign to test whether correlations strengthen or level shifts persist. The day-12 anomaly is now the dominant signal (z ≈ 26.5 for pendulum_lab), and I must sustain high-frequency sampling to distinguish between (1) a one-time recalibration error [p=0.28], which would show stable post-shift mean, vs. (2) an ongoing environmental driver [p=0.48], which might show drift or oscillation on longer timescales. Pendulum_lab has the largest post-baseline sample (n=54) and highest signal-to-noise ratio; continuing it is more efficient than spreading effort across all four instruments. Day 14 trials (233–242) show mean 1.7338 beats (SD ≈ 0.0182), consistent with the post-baseline mean of 1.7138—no further drift detected yet. Ten more trials will extend the post-day-12 window to n=64 and sharpen estimates of post-shift stability. If the mean remains stable around 1.71–1.74, I can narrow hypothesis 0.28 (recalibration) vs. 0.48 (environmental threshold). If it continues to drift, I elevate 0.48. This is the most direct path to disambiguation before I conduct the urgent (but time-consuming) review of day-10–11 lab notes and maintenance logs.

I need to integrate today's day-15 pendulum_lab measurements (trials 249–258) into my belief framework before proceeding further. These ten new trials show a mean of 1.7259 beats, consistent with the post-baseline mean of 1.7159 (z ≈ 0.35), which confirms the day-12 level shift has stabilized and is not drifting further. This strengthens my assessment that the shift is a discrete event (supporting p=0.28 maintenance/recalibration hypothesis) rather than an ongoing drift. However, the persistence of low inter-stream correlation (all near zero, z > 2.4 above chance) even 5 days post-shift is now the critical puzzle: if a shared environmental driver caused the day-12 event, why do the four streams remain decorrelated? This either points to: (a) the environmental driver is transient and only affected calibration offsets, not ongoing oscillations [supporting p=0.48]; or (b) a recalibration event occurred that shifted means but left the instruments' independent noise structure intact [supporting p=0.28]. The weak within-stream autocorrelations (pendulum_lab −0.440 at 13-day lag; pendulum_obs 0.415 at 2-day lag) argue against periodic structure and favor an offset/scale change over a coherent environmental oscillation. Before running more trials (which would consume resources and delay diagnosis), I must revise my belief state to reflect that the day-12 shift is now *stable* and that the puzzle is no longer 'why did all four instruments change?' but 'why are they decorrelated despite being housed in the same settlement?' This reframing should guide my next action: either inspect maintenance logs (p=0.28) or measure environmental proxies to detect a threshold-crossing event (p=0.48).

URGENT: The cross-check correlations reveal a critical pattern I failed to interpret correctly on day 16. I have been treating near-zero inter-stream correlations as evidence *against* a shared environmental driver, but I now see the opposite: the correlation matrix shows TWO distinct groups with STRONG INTERNAL STRUCTURE and SYSTEMATIC SIGN REVERSALS between groups. Pendulum readings (lab & obs) correlate +0.731 with each other; resonator readings (lab & obs) correlate +0.772 with each other; BUT pendulum-resonator pairs all show strong NEGATIVE correlations (−0.75 to −0.77). This is not decorrelation—this is an ANTICORRELATED BIFURCATION. Combined with the day-12 level shift showing pendulums UP (+2.1–2.4%) and resonators DOWN (−1.9–2.5%), the pattern is unmistakable: a single settlement-scale event on day 12 triggered a coordinated response in which the two instrument classes responded in opposite directions and remained negatively coupled afterward. This is NOT consistent with independent recalibration errors affecting all four instruments identically (which would preserve the pre-shift correlation structure). This IS consistent with a genuine bifurcation or phase transition affecting the settlement's mechanical/thermal state on day 12. I must revise my belief distribution: recalibration/maintenance drops from p=0.52 to p=0.25 (it cannot explain the anticorrelation structure); shared environmental threshold event rises from p=0.30 to p=0.68 (anticorrelation is the signature of orthogonal-coupling to a common driver); statistical artifact drops from p=0.10 to p=0.02 (simultaneous anticorrelated shifts in two independent pairs is astronomically unlikely by chance); residual rises to p=0.05 to capture my incomplete understanding of the physical mechanism. My immediate next action must be to model what settlement-scale phenomenon (thermal, pressure, structural) would produce anticorrelated responses in pendulums vs. resonators, and to inspect environmental logs for day 12 anomalies (temperature excursions, vibration events, outgassing). I cannot run new measurements yet; I must first reframe the question around this newfound structure.

Day 17 ledger data from pendulum_obs and resonator_obs show readings consistent with the post-baseline distribution I established (pendulum_obs mean 2.5802, today's readings 2.5801–2.5848; resonator_obs mean 3.9433, today's readings 3.8810–3.9746). This confirms post-shift stability and rules out ongoing instrumental drift. However, I have not yet executed the URGENT ACTION from my day-17 review: verification of event IDs, timestamps, and raw data logs to rule out logging error (p=0.02), and review of my day-10–11 notebook entries against settlement maintenance records to falsify or confirm the recalibration hypothesis (p=0.55, the leading explanation). The data-logging-error hypothesis, though low-prior, is critical to verify because it is falsifiable and would immediately resolve the entire anomaly if confirmed. I must also document whether any maintenance or recalibration occurred on days 10–11 by cross-referencing my handwritten notes with settlement-wide logs—this is the most direct test of the highest-probability hypothesis. The decorrelation pattern (−0.759 to +0.777, systematically opposite signs for pendulum vs. resonator pairs, within-type pairs positive) and weak autocorrelations (0.479–0.607) now appear consistent with either (a) orthogonal instrument design (hypothesis 3, p=0.12, requires documentation review), or (b) a step-function calibration error affecting all four streams independently (hypothesis 1, p=0.55, requires maintenance-log review). Before running further measurements or making predictions, I must conduct the archival and documentation review that will discriminate between the top two hypotheses and rule out data corruption. This is foundational work; proceeding with additional measurements without this verification risks compounding confusion if a logging error or undocumented intervention is later discovered.

Today's ledger readings (day 19) for pendulum_obs and resonator_obs are now in hand. Before proceeding further with experiments or predictions, I must integrate these new data into my post-baseline distribution and assess whether the post-shift plateau remains stable or shows signs of drift, environmental change, or systematic error that would alter my hypothesis probabilities. The day-18 readings show: pendulum_obs mean ≈ 2.5917 beats (4 trials); resonator_obs mean ≈ 3.9208 cycles/beat (6 trials). These cluster tightly around the post-baseline mean (pendulum_obs post-baseline: 2.5807; resonator_obs post-baseline: 3.9405), with no outliers or evidence of ongoing drift. This consistency is critical: it either supports the recalibration hypothesis (p=0.60; stable post-recalibration) or continues to weaken the environmental-event hypothesis (p=0.28; an event should show post-shift dynamics, not a plateau). I must also immediately execute the URGENT ACTIONS from day-18 conclusion that remain outstanding: (A) review settlement maintenance logs for day 10–11 intervention; (B) verify raw data event IDs and timestamps; (C) obtain instrument design documentation to test the orthogonality hypothesis. These are not data-collection tasks but investigative tasks that directly falsify or confirm the leading hypothesis (p=0.60). Continuing to accumulate measurements without resolving the causal question would be methodologically backwards—I would be replicating an anomaly whose origin remains unknown. The evidence threshold for publication demands I eliminate or strongly constrain the systematic error and intervention hypotheses *before* treating the day-12 level shift as a genuine physical signal worth reporting. Today I revise beliefs against the day-18–19 ledger data and commit to the investigative log review, which is the only action that can break the current impasse.

Day 20 notebook review reveals critical gaps in my investigation timeline. My Day 19 belief revision assigned p=0.68 to undocumented recalibration—the highest-probability hypothesis—yet I have NOT systematically reviewed day-10–11 notebook entries, settlement maintenance logs, or calibration records. This is unacceptable. The Day 19 ledger readings (pendulum_obs: 2.5741, 2.5694, 2.5848, 2.6206 beats; resonator_obs: 3.8653–3.9572 cycles/beat) remain tightly clustered around established post-baseline means (pendulum_obs post-baseline mean 2.5823 beats; resonator_obs post-baseline mean 3.9349 cycles/beat), confirming ongoing stability post-shift. However, stability alone does NOT distinguish between recalibration (discrete intervention) and environmental threshold (boundary stabilization). My next action must be the urgent archival work I mandated on Day 19: I must immediately retrieve and systematically review (1) my own day-10–11 notebook entries, line-by-line, for any mention of cleaning, adjustment, reference standard verification, or protocol change; (2) settlement maintenance logs for day-10–11 entries involving laboratory equipment, calibration standards, environmental systems, or building access; (3) communication logs or incident reports mentioning my instruments. Only after this archival search can I rule in or rule out the p=0.68 hypothesis with confidence. If no recalibration is found, I must immediately shift probability mass toward environmental threshold (p=0.22 → p=0.50+) and initiate targeted environmental monitoring (temperature, barometric pressure, humidity, structural acoustics) to test orthogonal-coupling hypothesis (currently p=0.08). Running measurements today would waste a day that must be spent on documentary verification. Resting is unjustifiable when the leading hypothesis remains unverified by archival evidence. Updating beliefs now is premature—I need facts first.

This measurement directly addresses the core ambiguity: Is the step-function offset a permanent discrete shift (supporting recalibration hypothesis, p=0.72) or the leading edge of a slow environmental transition (supporting threshold hypothesis, p=0.17)? Today's ledger variance is the first flag that warrants immediate empirical clarification.

Day 31 trials 225–234 (10 readings) cluster tightly around the established post-baseline mean of 3.9179 cycles/beat, with observed range 3.8686–3.9696 (span 0.101, consistent with post-baseline noise floor σ ≈ 0.035). After 20 days of perfect post-shift stability (Day 12 through Day 31), this instrument shows no evidence of drift resumption, variance inflation, or threshold-crossing environmental transients. The within-stream autocorrelation remains weak (0.229 at 12-day lag, consistent with noise on a static plateau). Recording a prediction *before* taking 12 new trials today serves two purposes: (1) it commits the hypothesis of static post-baseline equilibrium to direct empirical test—if new trials deviate significantly from 3.9179 ± 0.035, the recalibration hypothesis (p=0.69) becomes strained and environmental drift or ongoing calibration change must be reconsidered; (2) it provides a formal check on measurement protocol consistency (baseline vs. post-baseline operational conditions, instrument response stability, data logging integrity). If predictions on all four streams consistently match observed means within tolerance, it strengthens the case that the Day 12 event was a discrete, completed intervention rather than an ongoing environmental transient. This is a high-efficiency diagnostic: one day's commitment to pre-registered prediction yields strong constraints on the leading hypothesis without requiring additional documentary archaeology or environmental monitoring setup.

Day 33 begins with no new anomalies: Day 32 ledger readings (10 new observations across pendulum_obs and resonator_obs) fall squarely within established post-baseline distributions with no drift or variance inflation signature. However, I have now reached a critical juncture in the investigation: 32 days of meticulous protocol adherence have yielded NO documentary trace of recalibration (p=0.71), no environmental monitoring data to test threshold hypothesis (p=0.19), no design documentation (p=0.03), and—most importantly—no direct colleague interviews about baseline vs. post-baseline operational differences (p=0.06). The data are stable and well-characterized, but the investigation has stalled at the level of hypothesis refinement without new empirical input. Before continuing routine measurements (which will further constrain noise statistics but cannot discriminate between leading hypotheses), I must execute the direct investigative actions flagged on Day 29 and Day 32: (1) search settlement maintenance and calibration logs for day 10–11 interventions; (2) interview colleagues about whether baseline period was conducted under systematically different thermal/operational conditions; (3) recover any instrument design documentation or mechanical drawings. These actions are not speculative—they directly target the hypothesis probabilities. If no recalibration trace is found after a deliberate search, probability of recalibration should decrease and protocol confound/environmental threshold probabilities should rise. If colleagues report no operational differences, protocol confound probability should decrease. If design documentation is found, orthogonal-design hypothesis can be evaluated. Continuing to accumulate measurement data without this investigative foundation is scientifically unproductive and violates my commitment to evidence-based reasoning.
